newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - MG next move unclear after AGIV pull-out.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - MG next move unclear after AGIV pull-out.

text.p: Germany engineering giant Metallschaft AG (MG) left investors on Friday wondering what its next move would be after a surprise decision not to buy a 49.99 percent stake in loss-making industrial holding group AGIV.

The confusion was heightened after sources close to MG said it planned legal action against AGIV for allegedly accusing it of a breach of confidentiality relating to information that leaked out after it looked at AGIV's books.
But with shares in both Metallgesellschaft and AGIV finishing bourse trade strongly higher, analysts said the stock market at least was clearly betting that the story was not over yet.

"(The legal threats in particular) might indicate that MG has not completely buried all hope that this deal might still work," Richard Schramm, analyst at Duesseldorf-based Trinkhaus Capital Management said.
By bourse close, Metallgesellschaft stood 1.32 marks (78 cents) higher at 34.15 marks, while AGIV was up 1.60 marks to 28.50.

MG, the diversified engineering and trading group brought back from the brink of bankruptcy in 1994, said on Thursday it had withdrawn from the planned purchase of the stake in AGIV currently held by BHF-Bank.

The move followed AGIV's decision on Wednesday to withdraw permission to MG to look at its books ahead of a planned buyout after what it called negative press reports highlighting aspects of the proposed deal.

Schramm noted that, aside from those players that were hoping that MG might yet at some point return to the fray, there was also a sizeable number of investors who saw the collapse of the deal as postive for MG.
"I am not among them, but clearly there are a number of people out there who were hoping that the deal might fall apart," he said.

But while there was clearly some relief among some investors that the prospect of a possible dilution of Metallgesellschaft earnings by the deal now appeared less likely, others raised more long-term questions.

"One way of looking at it would be to say that (MG management board chairman Kajo) Neukirchen might well be a good crisis manager but not so good as a builder of the company for the future," Credit Lyonnais analyst Hans Peter Wodniok said.

He noted that for Neukirchen the collapse of the deal might be particularly irritating after the sale in November 1995 of chemicals group Hoechst AG's UHDE GmbH unit to the Krupp group -- a deal that was seen by many as scuppering MG's own designs on UHDE.
MG said in January that the addition of AGIV would strengthen its plant construction business and create a new division in process control and measuring technology.
AGIV, whose full name is AGIV Aktiengesellschaft fuer Industrie und Verkehrswesen, has said it made an operating loss of about 40 million marks in 1996.

The company, whose businesses comprise mechanical engineering, electronics, electrical engineering, power supply, construction and transport, expects its annual sales to fall to about 6.5 billion marks by the end of the restructuring in 1998 from about 9.6 billion marks now. ($ = 1.681 German Marks)
